title: STL and Iterators
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand half-open ranges, iterator categories, and why algorithms like std::sort couple to iterator capability rather than container type.

phases.goal: Establish the STL's four pillars and iterators as the cursor abstraction that decouples algorithms from containers.

must_hit.point: The STL's four pillars are Containers, Iterators, Algorithms, and Function Objects (functors/lambdas), with allocators managing memory behind the scenes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the four named pillars and may mention allocators as the behind-the-scenes fifth.

must_hit.point: Algorithms operate on iterators rather than containers directly, so one algorithm (e.g. std::sort) works for any container whose iterators support the required operations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States decoupling: no per-container sort; iterators are the glue.

must_hit.point: An iterator provides a pointer-like interface (*, ++, and usually ==/!=) so algorithms traverse a sequence without knowing whether it lives in a vector, list, stream, or raw array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines iterator as pointer-like cursor/abstraction over container storage.

must_hit.point: STL ranges are half-open [begin, end): begin is included, end is excluded and must never be dereferenced—it is a one-past-the-last sentinel.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains [begin, end), empty when begin==end, and that *end() is undefined behaviour.

probes: What are the four pillars of the STL, and how do iterators let one algorithm work across different containers?
What does end() point to, and why must you never dereference it?

hints.1: Think bookmark into a container, not the container's storage layout.
hints.2: Name Containers, Iterators, Algorithms, Function Objects; then explain half-open [begin, end).
hints.3: end() is one-past-the-last (sentinel); empty means begin==end; *v.end() is UB like reading past an array.

phases.goal: Check command of accessors, const-correctness, the category hierarchy, and portable helpers in <iterator>.

must_hit.point: Containers expose begin/end (mutating), cbegin/cend (always read-only), and rbegin/rend / crbegin/crend for reverse traversal where ++ walks backwards.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes forward vs reverse and mutating vs const accessors from the table.

must_hit.point: std::begin/std::end free functions work for STL containers and built-in arrays; prefer them in generic code because member .begin() fails on raw arrays.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions free begin/end, arrays lacking members, and range-based for using free-function lookup.

must_hit.point: iterator allows read/write of the element; const_iterator allows only reading—and const_iterator is not the same as a const iterator (const iterator cannot be reseated but may still allow *it = value).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates element constness from iterator-object constness; notes iterator→const_iterator conversion is one-way.

must_hit.point: Classic iterator categories are Input, Output, Forward, Bidirectional, Random-Access; Contiguous (C++17/C++20) refines Random-Access with contiguous storage—list is bidirectional, vector is contiguous/random-access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the hierarchy and contrasts list vs vector; may note std::sort needs random-access.

must_hit.point: std::advance mutates in place; std::next/std::prev return a new iterator; std::distance returns hop count—O(1) for random-access, O(N) (or O(|n|) for advance) otherwise; prev requires bidirectional.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares mutate-vs-return and complexity by category; states prev needs bidirectional.

probes: Name the iterator categories and which category std::list versus std::vector provide.
What is the difference between a const_iterator and a const iterator?
When would you use std::advance versus std::next, and what is their complexity?

hints.1: Categories form a ladder of capabilities algorithms demand.
hints.2: Input/Output → Forward → Bidirectional → Random-Access → Contiguous; helpers abstract category gaps.
hints.3: list: bidirectional (no it+n); vector: random-access/contiguous; advance mutates O(1)/O(|n|); next non-mutating; prev needs bidirectional.

phases.goal: Surface when category requirements and adaptor choice force different APIs or complexity.

must_hit.point: std::sort requires random-access iterators, so it cannot be used on std::list; use list::sort instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links sort's random-access demand to list's bidirectional-only iterators.

must_hit.point: Writing it+n or end-begin is legal only for random-access; <iterator> helpers give one spelling for every category with complexity that degrades gracefully.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts operator+ on vector with std::advance on list.

must_hit.point: front_inserter requires push_front (deque/list, not vector) and reverses apparent copy order because each insert lands at the front; prefer back_inserter or inserter at end() for stable order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States push_front requirement and order-reversal trap versus back_inserter.

probes: Why can't you call std::sort on a std::list, and what do you use instead?
Why prefer std::advance/std::distance over it+n / end-begin in generic code?

hints.1: Match algorithm requirements to what the iterator can do.
hints.2: Random-access enables O(1) jumps; bidirectional walks; adaptors change assignment into insert.
hints.3: std::sort needs random-access → list::sort; helpers O(1) on random-access else linear; front_inserter reverses order.

phases.goal: Apply iterators in real code: adaptors, streams, range-based for, invalidation, and C++20 ranges.

must_hit.point: Inserter adaptors turn *it=value into push_back (back_inserter), push_front (front_inserter), or insert(hint,value) (inserter)—so std::copy can append into an empty destination.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains back_inserter with copy into empty vector; may mention set/map via inserter.

must_hit.point: Stream iterators adapt iostreams: istream_iterator is a single-pass input iterator with default-constructed end-of-stream sentinel; ostream_iterator writes via << on assignment.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes copy from istream_iterator to back_inserter and ostream_iterator with delimiter.

must_hit.point: Range-based for is syntactic sugar over begin/end (members or ADL free functions); the type only needs iterators supporting !=, ++, and *.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Desugars for (T x : range) into begin/end loop; mentions by-value vs reference binding.

must_hit.point: Mutating a container can invalidate iterators (e.g. vector push_back may reallocate); using an invalidated iterator or dereferencing end() is undefined behaviour—re-obtain iterators after mutations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives vector reallocation example and rule-of-thumb that list/map typically invalidate only erased elements.

must_hit.point: reverse_iterator::base() does not point at the same element as *rit—it is the forward iterator one past the element rit dereferences (classic off-by-one).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States base() is one past *rit when mixing reverse and forward iterators.

probes: How would you use std::copy to append into an empty vector without pre-sizing it?
What does a range-based for loop expand to under the hood?
What happens to existing iterators if you push_back into a vector that reallocates?

hints.1: Adaptors and free begin/end let algorithms talk to containers, arrays, and streams uniformly.
hints.2: back_inserter for append; range-for uses begin/end; invalidation is dangling after storage moves.
hints.3: std::copy(..., std::back_inserter(dest)); for desugars to begin!=end ++; after vector realloc *old_it is UB; rit.base() is one past *rit.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: std::sort needs random-access iterators; std::list only provides bidirectional, so use member list::sort instead of std::sort on list.

tradeoffs.topic: it + n / end - begin vs std::advance / std::distance
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arithmetic is only for random-access; helpers work for every category—O(1) on random-access, O(N) or O(|n|) otherwise—so prefer helpers in generic code.
Free std::begin/std::end work for containers and built-in arrays; member .begin() fails on raw arrays; prefer free functions in generic code (range-based for uses them).
back_inserter uses push_back and preserves copy order; front_inserter needs push_front (not vector) and reverses apparent order; use inserter at end() if you need stable order without push_back.

tradeoffs.topic: iterator vs const_iterator (and vs const iterator)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: iterator can mutate elements; const_iterator cannot write through *; a const iterator cannot be reseated (++ fails) but may still allow *it=value—orthogonal axes of constness.

tradeoffs.topic: Pre-C++20 iterator pairs vs C++20 ranges
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ranges let algorithms take a whole range (std::ranges::sort(v)) instead of begin/end pairs; under the hood a range still has begin and end—half-open ranges, categories, and invalidation still apply.

gotchas.correction: They are sentinels (one-past-the-last / one-before-first), not elements; *v.end() is undefined behaviour.
const_iterator forbids writing through *it but can be advanced; const iterator cannot be reseated but may still allow *it = value if it is a mutating iterator type.

gotchas.trap: Calling std::prev on a pure forward or input iterator
gotchas.correction: std::prev requires bidirectional or stronger; std::next works from input iterators upward.

gotchas.trap: Assuming reverse_iterator::base() refers to the same element as *rit
gotchas.correction: base() is the underlying forward iterator one past the element the reverse iterator dereferences—mixing directions without adjusting causes off-by-one bugs.

gotchas.trap: Using front_inserter and expecting copy to preserve order
gotchas.correction: Each push_front lands at the front, so relative order reverses; prefer back_inserter or inserter at end() for stable order.

gotchas.trap: std::distance(first, last) with unreachable or wrong-order iterators on non-random-access ranges
gotchas.correction: last must be reachable by incrementing first; unrelated containers or wrong order is undefined behaviour.

gotchas.trap: Using iterators after a mutating operation that may reallocate or erase
gotchas.correction: Invalidated iterators are UB to use; after push_back/erase/insert, re-obtain iterators from return values or begin() again—rules vary by container.
It uses operator>>, so formatting/locale and leftover characters in the stream can stop typed reads early.
